title: C++ foundations & the standard library
description: Build confidence with C++20, complexity, iterators, containers, and standard algorithms.
recognition: Choose vector for contiguous storage, map for ordered lookup, unordered_map for average constant-time lookup, and priority_queue for repeated extremes. Sort before searching a range.
pitfalls: Iterator invalidation; accidental map insertion with operator[]; overflow in int; comparators must define a strict weak ordering.

exercises.title: Implement a small dynamic array
exercises.prompt: Implement push_back, pop_back, size, and indexed access for integers using a heap-allocated buffer. Double capacity when full. Then solve the same task using std::vector and compare amortized complexity. Test empty, growth, and repeated pop cases.
hints: Track size separately from capacity.
Allocate a larger buffer before copying and releasing the old one.
exercises.solution: Geometric growth makes a sequence of n appends O(n). Indexed access is O(1). Use RAII (std::unique_ptr<int[]>) to release memory; reject out-of-range access and popping an empty array.

title: Sorting & frequency counting
description: Turn unordered input into structure using comparators and frequency tables.
recognition: Ordering exposes adjacent equal values, rank, and greedy choices. Small alphabets often need only an array of counts.
pitfalls: Subtracting values in a comparator can overflow. Never use <= as the comparator.

exercises.title: Stable score ordering
exercises.prompt: Given (name, score, arrival) records, order scores descending while preserving arrival order on ties. Implement with stable_sort, then with an explicit tie-breaker.
hints: A comparator answers whether x must come before y.
For equal scores return false in both directions with stable_sort.
exercises.solution: Both variants take O(n log n). Verify all-equal scores, negative scores, and already sorted input. Explain why a non-strict comparator violates the sorting contract.

title: Two pointers
description: Replace nested scans with coordinated movement through a sequence.
recognition: Look for sorted pairs, in-place compaction, merging, or palindromes. Prove why moving one pointer discards only impossible candidates.
pitfalls: Two pointers are not valid for every pair search; sortedness or another monotonic property is essential.

exercises.title: Merge without extra sorting
exercises.prompt: Merge two sorted arrays and remove duplicates in O(n+m). Handle an empty input and duplicates within each input.
hints: Always consume the smaller front item.
Emit only when the output is empty or the last emitted value differs.
exercises.solution: Each pointer advances at most its input length. O(n+m) time and O(n+m) output space. Contrast with concatenating and sorting.

title: Fixed & variable sliding windows
description: Maintain a summary while a contiguous interval moves.
recognition: Use fixed windows for exact lengths. Variable windows need a condition you can restore by shrinking from the left.
pitfalls: A sum-based shrink rule fails with negative numbers. Distinguish exactly k from at most k.

exercises.title: Longest interval with at most k distinct values
exercises.prompt: Return the length and endpoints of the longest contiguous interval containing at most k distinct integers. Include k=0.
hints: Maintain frequencies and the number of nonzero frequencies.
Shrink until distinct <= k, then update the best interval.
exercises.solution: Each element enters and leaves once: O(n) expected time with a hash map. Removing a key at zero keeps distinct counts accurate.

title: Prefix sums & difference arrays
description: Answer range queries and batch interval updates using cumulative structure.
recognition: Static range sums are differences of prefixes. Many additive interval updates become two boundary changes.
pitfalls: Choose one interval convention and document it. Use 64-bit sums.

exercises.title: Batch range additions
exercises.prompt: Start with n zeros. Apply q updates adding x to inclusive [l,r]. Return the final array without looping over each interval.
hints: Add x at l and subtract x at r+1.
Recover values with one prefix scan.
exercises.solution: Use n+1 or n+2 storage for the right boundary. O(n+q) time. Test a single point, the full range, and overlapping updates.

title: Binary search & searching the answer
description: Find boundaries and optimize a monotonic feasibility predicate.
recognition: Search a sorted sequence or the smallest feasible answer. Write the predicate before writing the search.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors; midpoint overflow; feasibility must be monotonic.

exercises.title: Implement lower_bound
exercises.prompt: Return the first index with a[i] >= x in a sorted vector, or n if none. Do not call lower_bound in your implementation; compare against it in tests.
hints: Use the half-open interval [lo,hi).
Maintain that every index before lo is too small.
exercises.solution: An empty vector needs no special branch. O(log n) comparisons. Test duplicates and targets outside the range.

title: String manipulation & palindromes
description: Build safe string transformations, matching scans, and palindrome checks.
recognition: Decide whether the problem needs character counts, positional order, or both.
pitfalls: Byte-based std::string is not a Unicode character sequence. Cast to unsigned char before calling cctype functions.

exercises.title: Run-length encode and decode
exercises.prompt: For lowercase ASCII input, encode each run as (character,count) pairs and reconstruct the original. Define behavior for the empty string.
hints: Flush the previous run when the character changes.
Using structured pairs avoids ambiguity between counts and characters.
exercises.solution: Both operations are linear in input/output size. State a maximum decoded size before allocating; malformed or enormous counts should be rejected.

title: Hash maps & rolling hashes
description: Use fast lookup for complements, signatures, and substring fingerprints.
recognition: Repeated membership queries suggest hash maps. Rolling hashes support substring comparisons with collision risk.
pitfalls: Hash equality is not proof of string equality. Prefer deterministic algorithms where correctness requires it.

exercises.title: Anagram groups
exercises.prompt: Group lowercase words by an array of 26 character counts. Compare that signature with sorted-string signatures.
hints: Anagrams have identical multiplicities.
Serialize counts with separators or use an array comparator.
exercises.solution: Counting signatures take O(total characters) plus map overhead. Sorting each word costs O(L log L). Keep a deterministic signature instead of a lossy hash-only key.

title: Recursion, backtracking & divide and conquer
description: Explore choices carefully and split independent subproblems.
recognition: Backtracking needs choose, recurse, undo. Divide and conquer needs a base case and a correct merge.
pitfalls: Forgetting to undo state leaks decisions into sibling branches. Bound exponential work before running.

exercises.title: Generate balanced parentheses
exercises.prompt: Generate all balanced sequences with n pairs. Prune invalid prefixes rather than generating all 2^(2n) strings.
hints: Track opened and closed counts.
You may close only when closed < opened.
exercises.solution: Every prefix has at least as many opens as closes. Output-sensitive complexity is proportional to the Catalan number times n. n=0 has one empty sequence.

title: Greedy choices & intervals
description: Learn to justify a local choice with an exchange argument.
recognition: Scheduling non-overlapping intervals suggests earliest finishing time. Greedy choices need a proof, not just a plausible sort order.
pitfalls: Picking shortest duration or earliest start is not generally optimal for maximum interval count.

exercises.title: Interval scheduling counterexamples
exercises.prompt: Implement earliest-finish scheduling. Construct counterexamples for earliest-start and shortest-duration strategies. Define whether touching endpoints overlap.
hints: Replace the first chosen job with one finishing no later.
Apply the same argument to the remaining suffix.
exercises.solution: The exchange argument preserves room for all later intervals. Sorting dominates at O(n log n). Test nested and identical intervals.

title: Bits, modular arithmetic & number theory
description: Work with masks, divisibility, fast powers, and combinatorial counts.
recognition: Bitmasks model small subsets; Euclid handles gcd; repeated squaring handles huge exponents.
pitfalls: Signed shifts and overflow can be undefined. Modular inverse is not available for every divisor.

exercises.title: Sieve and factor queries
exercises.prompt: Precompute the smallest prime factor for every integer up to N, then answer prime-factorization queries.
hints: Mark a number only the first time it is reached.
Repeatedly divide by its smallest prime factor.
exercises.solution: A classic sieve takes O(N log log N); factorization takes O(log x) divisions. Handle 1 separately. Compare gcd against std::gcd on small examples.

title: Linked lists, stacks, queues & heaps
description: Implement the data structures behind familiar STL interfaces.
recognition: Use a stack for nested work, a queue for arrival order, and a heap for repeated minimum/maximum selection.
pitfalls: Raw owning pointers require careful lifetime management. Prefer unique_ptr for ownership and avoid reference cycles.

exercises.title: Implement a binary min-heap
exercises.prompt: Implement push, top, and pop over a vector. Maintain parent <= children after every operation and compare with priority_queue.
hints: Push bubbles a value upward.
Pop replaces the root with the last item, then sifts downward.
exercises.solution: Push/pop take O(log n), top takes O(1). Reject operations on an empty heap. A bottom-up heapify builds a heap in O(n).

title: Monotonic stacks & queues
description: Keep only candidates that can still influence a future answer.
recognition: Next smaller/greater elements suggest a monotonic stack. Window extrema suggest a deque of indices.
pitfalls: Equal values change strict versus non-strict answers. Expire indices that leave the window.

exercises.title: Sliding maximum from scratch
exercises.prompt: Implement an O(n) sliding-window maximum with a deque. Return an empty result for an invalid window length.
hints: Remove expired indices from the front.
Remove dominated values from the back.
exercises.solution: Each index enters and exits at most once, giving O(n) total work. Explain why a smaller earlier value cannot beat a larger later one.

title: Dynamic programming: states & transitions
description: Turn repeated subproblems into a state table with explicit invariants.
recognition: Define exactly what dp[state] means, list transitions, choose base cases, and derive an evaluation order.
pitfalls: Memoizing an incomplete state yields wrong answers. Distinguish impossible states from valid zero values.

exercises.title: Stairs with forbidden steps
exercises.prompt: Count ways to reach step n using jumps of 1,2,3 while avoiding blocked steps. Solve first recursively with memoization, then bottom-up.
hints: Let dp[i] count paths ending exactly at i.
Blocked states have zero ways; dp[0]=1 unless the start is blocked.
exercises.solution: O(n) time, O(n) space or O(1) rolling state. Compare both methods on small n. State whether counts need a modulus.

title: Grid DP
description: Track paths and costs through a directed grid of states.
recognition: Moves restricted to right/down give a natural topological evaluation order.
pitfalls: Blocked starts or ends matter. Initialize borders consistently and avoid adding to infinity.

exercises.title: Minimum path with reconstruction
exercises.prompt: Find a minimum-cost right/down path and return the sequence of cells, not just the cost.
hints: Store the chosen predecessor for each reachable cell.
Backtrack from the destination and reverse the path.
exercises.solution: O(hw) time and space. If costs tie, define a deterministic tie-break. Test a single row, one cell, and an unreachable destination.

title: Knapsack & subset sums
description: Choose items under a budget and distinguish 0/1 from unbounded use.
recognition: Capacity-based and value-based states trade dimensions. The iteration direction determines whether an item can be reused.
pitfalls: Forward iteration accidentally turns 0/1 knapsack into unbounded knapsack.

exercises.title: 0/1 versus unbounded knapsack
exercises.prompt: Implement both variants and construct an input where a forward 0/1 loop returns an impossible answer.
hints: Use one item of weight 2 and value 3 with capacity 4.
Descending capacity preserves the previous-item layer.
exercises.solution: O(nW) time and O(W) space. Explain pseudo-polynomial complexity and when value-indexed DP is preferable.

title: Subsequence DP & LIS
description: Align sequences or maintain the best possible tail of each length.
recognition: LCS/edit distance compare two prefixes. LIS uses smaller tails to preserve future extension opportunities.
pitfalls: A tails array is not necessarily an actual subsequence. Strict and non-decreasing LIS use different bounds.

exercises.title: Reconstruct an LIS
exercises.prompt: Return the indices of one strictly increasing subsequence of maximum length in O(n log n).
hints: Track the index associated with each tail length.
Store the predecessor index when placing each value.
exercises.solution: Follow predecessors from the final tail and reverse. Use lower_bound for strict LIS. Test duplicate values and decreasing input.

title: Interval DP & games
description: Solve ranges by combining smaller ranges or choosing an endpoint.
recognition: State dp[l][r] when the remaining work is a contiguous interval. Iterate by increasing length.
pitfalls: Separate score difference from total score. A split transition may require cubic time.

exercises.title: Optimal take-from-ends game
exercises.prompt: Two players take a value from either end. Return the optimal first-player score, allowing negative values.
hints: Use the current player’s score advantage as the state.
Total score and score difference determine the first player’s score.
exercises.solution: O(n²) time; O(n²) space or a carefully ordered rolling array. Do not assume choosing the larger endpoint is optimal.

title: Bitmask & subset DP
description: Use a mask when the chosen subset is part of the state.
recognition: Assignment, small-set routes, and subset partitioning often fit 2^n states.
pitfalls: Check n before allocating. Enumerating every submask across every mask costs O(3^n).

exercises.title: Assignment counting
exercises.prompt: Count perfect assignments for n<=20 given a compatibility matrix. Compare against permutation enumeration for n<=8.
hints: The number of set bits identifies the next person.
Only add an unused compatible job.
exercises.solution: O(n2^n) time, O(2^n) space. Set dp[0]=1. Use modular arithmetic when requested and unsigned masks for bit operations.

title: Digit DP & probability DP
description: Add only the state dimensions that influence future choices.
recognition: Digit constraints need position, tightness, and relevant prefix information. Expectations often follow E=1+weighted future expectations.
pitfalls: Leading zeroes change digit constraints. An expectation equation with self-loops must be algebraically rearranged.

exercises.title: Count digit sums in a range
exercises.prompt: Count integers in [L,R] whose digit sum is divisible by D. Decide explicitly whether zero is included.
hints: Implement count_up_to(X), then subtract count_up_to(L-1).
Track tightness to avoid enumerating beyond X.
exercises.solution: O(number_of_digits * D * 10). Use brute force to validate small ranges. Include L=0 and powers of ten.

title: Graph traversal, BFS & bipartite graphs
description: Represent graphs and explore reachability, shortest unweighted paths, and coloring.
recognition: BFS gives fewest edges in an unweighted graph. DFS discovers components and structural relationships.
pitfalls: Mark BFS nodes when enqueuing. Deep recursive DFS may overflow the call stack.

exercises.title: Bipartite check with a witness
exercises.prompt: Color every component with two colors. If impossible, return an odd cycle using parent pointers.
hints: Neighbors need opposite colors.
A same-color edge joins two parent paths; find their common ancestor.
exercises.solution: O(V+E) time. Disconnected components, self-loops, and isolated vertices must be handled. Validate the witness has odd length.

title: Topological sorting & DAG DP
description: Order dependencies and propagate information along directed acyclic graphs.
recognition: An indegree-zero queue provides a dependency order. Fewer than V processed nodes implies a cycle.
pitfalls: Longest-path DP is not valid on arbitrary cyclic graphs. Ignore unreachable states.

exercises.title: Count paths in a DAG
exercises.prompt: Count paths from s to t modulo M and reject cyclic input. Return zero when t is unreachable.
hints: Topologically order all vertices first.
Initialize ways[s]=1 and propagate along each edge.
exercises.solution: O(V+E). Decide whether parallel edges represent distinct paths. A cycle elsewhere still violates the stated DAG input contract.

title: Disjoint sets & minimum spanning trees
description: Maintain connected components and connect them with minimum total edge cost.
recognition: Union-find tracks merging sets. Kruskal considers edges from cheapest to most expensive.
pitfalls: DSU does not support arbitrary deletions. An MST exists only when the graph is connected.

exercises.title: Implement DSU and Kruskal
exercises.prompt: Implement path compression and union by size. Return an MST’s total cost and its selected edges, or report disconnection.
hints: Count successful unions.
A connected graph requires exactly V-1 selected edges.
exercises.solution: O(E log E) sorting plus nearly constant amortized DSU operations. Use 64-bit totals and allow negative edge weights.

title: Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford & all-pairs paths
description: Choose a path algorithm based on weights and graph size.
recognition: Dijkstra requires nonnegative weights; Bellman–Ford handles negative edges; Floyd–Warshall suits small dense graphs.
pitfalls: Discard stale heap entries. Negative cycles require reachability reasoning. Never add weights to an infinite distance.

exercises.title: Shortest path reconstruction
exercises.prompt: Implement Dijkstra with predecessor tracking. Return the route and cost, or an explicit unreachable result.
hints: Update parent only when improving a distance.
Stop reconstruction at the source; reverse the path.
exercises.solution: O((V+E)log V). Validate every weight is nonnegative. Test parallel edges, zero weights, and a source equal to the target.

title: Trees, tree DP & rerooting
description: Aggregate subtrees and reuse results when changing the root.
recognition: Trees have one simple path between vertices. Postorder combines child states; rerooting moves information across an edge.
pitfalls: Avoid processing the parent as a child. A path-shaped tree may require iterative traversal.

exercises.title: All-root distance sums
exercises.prompt: Compute the sum of distances from every vertex to all others in O(n).
hints: First compute subtree sizes and the sum from one root.
Across u->v, sz[v] nodes get closer and n-sz[v] get farther.
exercises.solution: Two traversals, O(n) time and space. Use 64-bit answers. Verify on a chain, a star, and one vertex.

title: Binary lifting & lowest common ancestors
description: Precompute powers of parent jumps for ancestry and distance queries.
recognition: Repeated ancestor queries suggest binary lifting; LCA reduces path distance to depths.
pitfalls: Keep root ancestor entries valid. Allocate enough levels for the maximum depth.

exercises.title: Ancestor queries
exercises.prompt: Answer kth-ancestor queries, returning -1 when the ancestor does not exist. Then extend to LCA.
hints: Raise the deeper vertex to equal depth.
Lift both from the largest power downward while their ancestors differ.
exercises.solution: O(n log n) preprocessing and O(log n) per query. Handle k=0, the root, and k exceeding depth.

title: Fenwick trees, segment trees & sparse tables
description: Match the data structure to the operation and update model.
recognition: Fenwick supports additive prefixes, segment trees support associative merges, and sparse tables handle static idempotent queries.
pitfalls: A merge needs a correct identity. Lazy propagation must compose updates in the right order.
cpp_example:
void add(int i,long long x){for(++i;i<=n;i+=i&-i)bit[i]+=x;}
long long prefix(int i){long long s=0;for(;i;i-=i&-i)s+=bit[i];return s;}

exercises.title: Implement a range-sum library
exercises.prompt: Implement Fenwick point-add/range-sum and segment-tree point-set/range-min interfaces. Cross-check random operations against an array.
hints: Use half-open ranges at the API boundary.
A minimum-query identity can be numeric_limits<long long>::max().
exercises.solution: O(log n) updates/queries. Add a static sparse table for min and explain why overlapping blocks work for min but not sum. For offline Mo ordering, measure pointer movements and document its O((n+q)sqrt n) bound.

title: Tries, KMP & Z algorithm
description: Index shared prefixes and match patterns without rescanning text.
recognition: Tries organize dictionary prefixes. Prefix/Z arrays reuse already established character matches.
pitfalls: Reset KMP using failure links rather than restarting. For combined strings, choose a separator outside the alphabet.

exercises.title: Overlapping pattern matches
exercises.prompt: Implement KMP and return every start index, including overlaps. Compare with a naive matcher on randomized short strings.
hints: After a full match, continue from pi[m-1].
Define the empty-pattern behavior explicitly.
exercises.solution: O(n+m) time and O(m) state. For pattern aaa in aaaaa, return 0,1,2. Implement Z as a second linear-time solution.

title: Strongly connected components & 2-SAT
description: Compress mutual reachability into a DAG and model logical implications.
recognition: SCCs partition directed graphs. In 2-SAT, a variable and its negation cannot belong to the same SCC.
pitfalls: Reverse finishing order correctly in Kosaraju. Assignment direction depends on the SCC numbering convention.

exercises.title: Build the condensation graph
exercises.prompt: Compute SCCs with Kosaraju, deduplicate component edges, and verify the condensed graph is acyclic.
hints: First pass records finishing order.
Second pass traverses reversed edges in reverse finishing order.
exercises.solution: O(V+E), aside from optional edge deduplication. Test a fully strongly connected graph and isolated vertices. Preserve original-to-component mapping.

title: Bridges & articulation points
description: Find edges and vertices whose removal disconnects an undirected graph.
recognition: Discovery times and low-link values capture whether a subtree has a back edge to an ancestor.
pitfalls: Skip the parent edge ID, not every edge to the parent; parallel edges matter. DFS roots use a separate articulation rule.

exercises.title: Low-link implementation with multiedges
exercises.prompt: Return all bridges and articulation vertices. Support disconnected graphs, parallel edges, and self-loops.
hints: Track a unique ID for each undirected edge.
A DFS root is an articulation point only with more than one DFS child.
exercises.solution: O(V+E). Validate by brute-force edge and vertex removal on small graphs. The strict bridge inequality differs from the articulation inequality.

title: Euler paths, matching & network flow
description: Learn edge-covering traversals, pair assignments, and capacity-constrained routing.
recognition: Euler paths visit every edge; bipartite matching pairs vertices; residual networks allow flow to be revised.
pitfalls: An Euler trail also needs connectivity. Reverse residual edges are essential for rerouting previous decisions.

exercises.title: Bipartite matching via augmenting paths
exercises.prompt: Implement maximum bipartite matching, then model it as unit-capacity max flow and compare the answers.
hints: A DFS can reassign an already matched right vertex.
In the flow model, connect source->left and right->sink with capacity 1.
exercises.solution: Simple augmenting matching is O(VE). For larger graphs use Hopcroft–Karp or Dinic. Separately implement Hierholzer and verify every input edge is used exactly once.

title: Matrix exponentiation & DP optimizations
description: Recognize structured transitions and prove when optimization is valid.
recognition: Linear recurrences suggest matrix powers. Quadratic transitions may become lines, Monge arrays, or monotone optimal split points.
pitfalls: Do not apply divide-and-conquer or Knuth optimization without proving its assumptions. Overflow is common in cross-products.

exercises.title: Optimize a quadratic recurrence
exercises.prompt: Implement a brute-force DP for dp[i]=min(j<i){dp[j]+(h[i]-h[j])²+C}, then a Li Chao tree version. Differential-test small random arrays.
hints: Each previous state defines a line with slope -2*h[j].
Query at x=h[i], then add h[i]²+C.
exercises.solution: A Li Chao tree handles arbitrary query order in O(n log X). Use a discrete-coordinate version or a bounded domain, and 128-bit intermediate arithmetic. Explain when a monotone hull could be simpler.
